Fabiana, it's Greg Walsh from Sales. Look, I'll be direct. Our biggest customer in Chicago needs the keyboards on the fourteenth, not the twenty-first. I already promised them the fourteenth. I don't care how you do it. Put it on a plane, run extra shifts in Monterrey, whatever it takes. If we lose this account, that's going to be a supply chain problem, not a sales problem. And frankly, I'm tired of hearing about Penang. That was months ago. Call me back today.

Fabiana, it's Priya. I wanted to give you some feedback on the meeting with the CFO. First, well done. He pushed hard, and you kept a cool head. When he said the budget was a luxury, you didn't take it personally. You reframed it: not a cost, but insurance against another twelve days of lost supply. That changed the room. One small thing for next time. When he interrupted you the second time, you started to apologize. You don't need to. You can simply say, I'd rather finish the point, and then I'll take your question. He respects that. The result? He wants a revised number by Friday. That's not a yes, but it's a real door. And about Greg: I heard he called you. I'd rather you didn't solve that one alone, so please copy me on your reply.

Fabiana plans her callback to Greg. First, she hears Greg out and lets him vent about the Chicago customer. Then she validates the pressure: she understands the customer is pushing him hard. Next, she stands her ground: I'd rather we didn't promise the fourteenth. After that, she offers a solution: forty percent by air by the fourteenth, the rest by the twenty-first. Finally, she closes firmly: it's time we agreed on one date and kept it.
